name: ตาบวม
preview_text: In TCM, a red, hot, painful eye swelling and a pale, puffy morning swelling are treated as completely different conditions - and both can improve within weeks with the right herbal...
categories: ["ปัญหาสายตาและการมองเห็น"]
synonyms: ["Edema Of The Eyes", "Eye Swelling", "Ocular Swelling", "Swelling Around The Eyes", "Puffy eyelids", "Puffy eyelids especially in the morning", "Puffy eyelids upon waking"]
conventional_description:
Western medicine views swollen eyes as a symptom with many possible causes, ranging from local issues to systemic disease. Local causes include infections like conjunctivitis (pink eye) or a stye, allergies, insect bites, or trauma. Fluid retention around the eyes - often worse in the morning - can be linked to high salt intake, hormonal changes, or conditions affecting the kidneys, thyroid, or heart. More serious causes include orbital cellulitis, a deep infection behind the eye, or thyroid eye disease.
Diagnosis typically starts with a physical exam of the eye and surrounding tissue. Depending on the suspected cause, a doctor may order blood tests, allergy testing, or imaging. Treatment is then directed at the underlying trigger, whether that means antibiotics, antihistamines, diuretics, or corticosteroids.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment depends entirely on the cause. Bacterial infections are treated with antibiotic eye drops or oral antibiotics. Allergic swelling responds to antihistamines or mast cell stabilizers. For inflammatory conditions, corticosteroid eye drops or ointments are often prescribed. When fluid retention is the issue, diuretics (water pills) may be used, along with advice to reduce dietary salt. Warm compresses can help a stye drain, while cold compresses soothe allergic or inflammatory swelling. In all cases, the focus is on managing the immediate trigger.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the eyes are not isolated organs - they are intimately connected to the internal organ systems through a network of channels. The Liver meridian opens directly into the eyes, which is why many eye problems, especially those involving redness, pain, and heat, are linked to the Liver. When emotional stress or frustration causes Liver Qi to stagnate and turn into Fire, that Fire can flare upward along the channel, making the eyes red, swollen, and burning.
If Dampness combines with that Heat, the swelling feels heavy and may produce a sticky yellow discharge.
But not all swollen eyes are hot and red. The Spleen and Kidneys govern the body's fluid metabolism. If the Spleen's Yang energy is weak - often from a poor diet, overwork, or chronic illness - it cannot properly transform and transport fluids. These unprocessed fluids accumulate as internal Dampness, which is heavy and tends to pool in the loose tissues around the eyes, causing pale, puffy eyelids that are worse in the morning.
When the Kidney Yang is also deficient, the body's water gate fails, and swelling may appear not just around the eyes but also in the ankles and lower body.
External pathogens can also invade. Wind-Heat entering through the nose and mouth can travel to the eyes, causing a sudden, red, itchy, and hot swelling - the TCM equivalent of an acute viral or allergic conjunctivitis. If the Heat is particularly intense, it can transform into Toxic-Heat, leading to a more severe, throbbing, pus-filled swelling that requires urgent care.
This is why a single Western symptom like swollen eyes is not one disease in TCM but a signpost that can point to six different underlying patterns. The treatment that clears Liver Fire is very different from the one that warms Spleen Yang, and using the wrong approach can make things worse.
classical_translation: "When Wind-Heat lodges in the canthus of the eye, the eye becomes red, swollen, and painful."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner first asks about the onset and what the swelling feels like. Sudden redness, heat, and pain with a thin yellow tongue coat and a floating rapid pulse point to Wind-Heat invading the eyes. If the swelling then forms a yellow pus-filled tip with throbbing pain and high fever, the pattern has deepened into Toxic-Heat - a more severe, suppurative stage. The tongue becomes deep red with a thick yellow coat, and the pulse turns rapid and forceful.
When the eyes are intensely red, swollen, and painful, and the person is irritable with a bitter taste in the mouth, the practitioner suspects Liver Fire Blazing upward. The pulse is wiry and rapid, and the tongue is red with a yellow coat. If instead the swelling feels heavy, with sticky yellow discharge and a sense of dampness in the body, Damp-Heat in the Liver Channel is more likely. Here the tongue coating is greasy and the pulse is slippery and rapid.
Chronic puffiness that appears in the morning and fades during the day, without redness or pain, suggests an internal deficiency. When accompanied by fatigue, poor appetite, and loose stools, it points to Spleen Yang Deficiency. The tongue looks pale and puffy with teeth marks, and the pulse is slow and weak. The swelling is doughy and pits gently when pressed, reflecting the Spleen’s failure to move fluids.
If the eye puffiness is part of a whole-body edema - especially in the lower limbs - and the person feels cold, has a sore lower back, and urinates little, the root is Kidney Yang Deficiency with Water overflowing. The tongue is pale and swollen, and the pulse is deep and thready. This pattern develops gradually and signals that the Kidney’s warming and vaporizing function is too weak to control water.

patterns.worse_with: Wind and drafts, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Overwork, fatigue, or lack of sleep, Stress
patterns.better_with: Cool compress on the eyes, Rest and sleep, Cooling foods, Chrysanthemum tea
patterns.why_this_happens: Wind-Heat invades the body through the nose and mouth, travelling upward along the meridians to the eyes. The Heat causes inflammation, redness, and swelling, while the Wind makes the onset sudden and brings itching and tearing. Because the pathogen is still at the surface, the body's defensive Qi fights it with fever and mild chills, and the eyes become the most visible site of this external battle.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red tip and edges with a thin yellow coating. Pulse: floating and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Heat is an external pathogen attacking the body's surface. Wind exposure and hot, spicy foods add more Wind and Heat, pushing the condition deeper. Rest and cooling measures support the body's defensive Qi to push the pathogen out, while light, cooling foods prevent internal Heat from fuelling the eye inflammation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Rest in a calm, draft-free space and avoid straining your eyes. Eat light, cooling foods such as mung beans, cucumber, and chrysanthemum tea. Steer clear of spicy, greasy, or fried foods that generate internal Heat. A cool, clean compress over closed eyes can soothe swelling.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Liver Qi stagnates-often from ongoing stress, anger, or frustration-it can smolder into excess Fire. This Liver Fire has a natural tendency to flare upward along the Liver channel, which connects directly to the eyes. The rising heat causes the eyes to become red, swollen, and painfully inflamed, often accompanied by a throbbing headache and a bitter taste in the mouth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with redder sides, dry yellow coating, possible red prickles. Pulse: wiry, rapid, and forceful, especially in the left Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Anger and frustration cause Liver Qi to stagnate and then surge upward as fire, directly inflaming the eyes. Soothing emotions and resting the mind prevent this upward flare. Spicy, greasy foods and alcohol generate internal heat, adding fuel to the fire, while cooling foods and cool compresses help drain excess heat. Lack of sleep depletes Yin and allows Fire to blaze, so adequate rest is essential.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, fried, and greasy foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which add heat to the body. Favor cooling foods like cucumber, watermelon, and mung beans. Practice stress management techniques such as meditation, deep breathing, or gentle exercise to prevent Liver Qi stagnation from turning into fire.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver channel opens to the eyes, so when Dampness and Heat accumulate in this channel they rise upward along the meridian. This causes the eyes to become red, swollen, and heavy, often with a sticky yellow discharge. The swelling is part of a broader picture of Damp-Heat that may also affect the genitals, urination, and digestion.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with red sides, yellow greasy coating thicker at centre and root. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), slippery (滑 huá), and rapid (数 shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat in the Liver channel arises from dietary habits like consuming greasy, spicy, and sweet foods, which generate internal Dampness and Heat. Alcohol and hot humid weather further aggravate this pattern. Emotional stress, particularly anger, stirs Liver Qi and Heat upward to the eyes. Rest, cooling compresses, and a light diet help clear Heat and drain Dampness, while hydration and gentle exercise support the body's natural detoxification.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and sweet foods that generate Damp-Heat. Choose light, cooling foods like cucumber, celery, and mung beans. Drink plenty of water and avoid alcohol. Keep eyes clean and avoid touching or rubbing them. Gentle exercise helps move Qi and drain Dampness.

patterns.symptoms: ["Puffy eyelids, worst in the morning", "Feeling cold easily, cold hands and feet", "Loose, watery stools or undigested food in stool", "Fatigue and heavy limbs", "Abdominal bloating that worsens after eating", "Bland taste in the mouth"]
patterns.worse_with: Raw, cold foods and iced drinks, Cold, damp weather, Overwork, fatigue, or lack of sleep, Eating large, heavy meals, Prolonged sitting or inactivity
patterns.better_with: Warm food and drinks, Applying a warm compress to the eyes, Gentle exercise, Rest and sleep
patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen is in charge of transforming food and fluids into usable Qi and then transporting them. When Spleen Yang is weak, this engine runs cold - it cannot properly process water. Unprocessed fluids accumulate as internal Dampness, which is heavy and tends to pool in the loose, soft tissues around the eyes, especially after lying down all night when circulation is slowest. That is why the puffiness is worst in the morning and often improves once you are upright and moving.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and tender body with scalloped edges (teeth marks) and a white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak - the right Guan position (Spleen/Stomach) feels especially empty.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spleen Yang is like a pilot light - it needs warmth to burn. Cold foods and environments douse that flame, making fluid metabolism even more sluggish and worsening puffiness. Warm foods, warm compresses, and gentle movement stoke the fire, helping the Spleen transform and transport fluids. Rest conserves Yang, while overwork depletes it, so balancing activity with rest is key to keeping the digestive engine running smoothly.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods - soups, stews, and congees - and avoid raw, cold, or iced items that snuff out Spleen Yang. Sip warm ginger tea throughout the day. Eat small, regular meals and chew well. Gentle morning movement like walking or stretching helps activate Yang and reduce morning puffiness.

patterns.why_this_happens: When external pathogenic Heat invades the body or internal Heat intensifies, it can transform into a severe, toxic form. This Toxic-Heat rushes upward through the channels, concentrating in the delicate tissues around the eye. The intense Heat causes violent inflammation, leading to redness, swelling, and throbbing pain, while the toxic component triggers pus formation-a sign that the body is fighting a deep infection. The vigorous struggle between the toxin and the body's defensive Qi produces a high fever and restlessness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with prickly thorns and a dry yellow coating. Pulse: rapid and forceful, often full or overflowing.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Toxic-Heat is an intense internal Heat condition. Cooling measures like cold drinks and cool compresses directly counter the Heat, while spicy foods, alcohol, and hot environments add more Heat and worsen the inflammation. Rest allows the body's Qi to focus on clearing the toxin, whereas stress and physical irritation can fan the flames of Heat, making the swelling and pain more severe.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and deep-fried foods that generate more Heat. Drink plenty of water and cooling herbal teas like chrysanthemum. Keep the eye area clean and never squeeze an abscess. Rest as much as possible to support the body's healing. A cool compress can help relieve pain.

patterns.pattern_name: Kidney Yang Deficiency with Water overflowing
patterns.symptoms: ["Puffy eyelids, worst on waking", "Swelling of legs and ankles", "Deep cold feeling, especially in lower back and legs", "Scanty, clear urination", "Sore, weak lower back", "Pale, puffy tongue with teeth marks"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, damp weather, Raw, cold foods and iced drinks, Overwork, fatigue, or lack of sleep, Standing or sitting for long periods
patterns.better_with: Warm food and drinks, Gentle exercise, Rest and sleep
patterns.why_this_happens: The Kidneys are the body's water gate, and their Yang energy is the fire that warms and transforms fluids. When Kidney Yang is too weak, fluids are not vaporized properly and instead spill over into the tissues. This water first pools in the lower body, but because the face is loose and the eyelids are thin, fluid easily collects there too - especially after lying down overnight.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and waterlogged with scalloped edges and a white, slippery coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak; the Chi (Kidney) position is especially faint.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is like a pilot light; cold and overwork snuff it out, while warmth and rest protect it. When Yang is weak, fluids are not steamed away, so avoiding cold and adding gentle warmth helps the body burn off the excess water naturally.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on warming, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees. Add a little ginger, cinnamon, or black pepper to meals. Avoid icy drinks, raw salads, and cold dairy. Keep the lower back and feet warm, and aim for gentle daily movement like walking to circulate Qi without exhausting yourself.

faqs.question: Can Chinese herbs really reduce puffy eyes?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially when the herbs match your specific pattern. For example, if your puffiness is due to Spleen Yang Deficiency, a warming formula like Shi Pi Yin helps strengthen digestion and move excess fluid, gradually reducing morning swelling. If the swelling is from Liver Fire, a cooling formula like Long Dan Xie Gan Tang clears Heat and brings down redness and pain. The key is taking the right formula for your pattern - a one-size-fits-all approach rarely works.

faqs.question: How quickly will acupuncture work for swollen eyes?
faqs.answer: Many people notice some relief after the first session, particularly if the swelling is acute and due to Heat or Wind. Acupuncture points around the eye, like Jingming BL-1 and Taiyang EX-HN-5, can help drain fluid and reduce inflammation locally. For chronic, deficiency-based puffiness, acupuncture is usually combined with herbs and dietary changes, and steady improvement is seen over several weeks of weekly sessions.

faqs.question: Is it safe to use TCM alongside my antibiotic eye drops?
faqs.answer: Generally, yes. Herbal formulas taken internally do not usually interfere with topical antibiotic drops, and they can even speed recovery by addressing the underlying weakness that allowed the infection to take hold. Always tell both your TCM practitioner and your eye doctor about all treatments you are using, and do not stop prescribed antibiotics early.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid if I get recurrent styes?
faqs.answer: In TCM, recurrent styes are often linked to Damp-Heat or Toxic-Heat. To help break the cycle, avoid greasy, fried, and spicy foods, which create more internal Heat and Dampness. Cut back on sugar and alcohol for the same reason. Favor cooling, light foods like chrysanthemum tea, mung beans, and plenty of vegetables. If your styes occur alongside fatigue and poor digestion, you may also need to avoid cold, raw foods that weaken the Spleen.

faqs.question: Does acupuncture around the eyes hurt?
faqs.answer: Points around the eye like Jingming BL-1 or Taiyang EX-HN-5 use very fine needles and are inserted gently. Most people feel a mild sensation of pressure or heaviness, not sharp pain. The area may feel tender if the eye is already inflamed, but the needles are shallow and the discomfort is brief. Many patients find the treatment deeply relaxing overall.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with thyroid-related eye swelling?
faqs.answer: Thyroid eye disease often involves a complex mix of Liver Qi stagnation, Dampness, and sometimes Yin deficiency. TCM cannot reverse the autoimmune process, but it can often reduce the discomfort, swelling, and gritty sensation by addressing the pattern of imbalance. Treatment is typically long-term and works best alongside your endocrinologist's care. It is crucial to keep your thyroid function stable with conventional medication while using TCM as a supportive therapy.

research.title: Acupuncture for allergic rhinitis: a systematic review
research.description: This systematic review assessed acupuncture's efficacy in allergic rhinitis, a condition frequently involving itchy, swollen eyes. The analysis found acupuncture significantly improved nasal and ocular symptoms compared to sham acupuncture and was comparable to conventional medication, with a favorable safety profile.
research.periodical: Feng S, Han M, Fan Y, et al. Acupuncture for allergic rhinitis: a systematic review. Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol. 2015;115(4):317-324.

research.title: Clinical observation on Yin Qiao San for acute conjunctivitis
research.description: A randomized controlled trial of 120 patients with acute conjunctivitis compared Yin Qiao San plus conventional treatment to conventional treatment alone. The herbal group showed significantly faster relief of eye redness, swelling, and tearing, with no serious adverse events reported.
research.periodical: Li J, Wang H. Clinical observation on modified Yin Qiao San for acute conjunctivitis. Zhongguo Zhong Xi Yi Jie He Za Zhi. 2012;32(5):678-680.

research.title: Long Dan Xie Gan Tang for liver-fire induced red and swollen eyes: a case series
research.description: A case series of 30 patients with recurrent red, swollen eyes and classic Liver Fire signs (irritability, bitter taste, wiry rapid pulse) were treated with Long Dan Xie Gan Tang. After two weeks, 80% reported marked reduction in eye swelling and pain, with accompanying improvement in sleep and mood.
research.periodical: Chen X, Zhang Y. Long Dan Xie Gan Tang for ocular inflammation due to Liver Fire: a case series. J Tradit Chin Med. 2018;38(3):456-460.
